No forms, no commitments, just a direct conversation about your business and what it needs. Book Your Free 30-Minute Call Or explore our Business Advisory and Startup Structuring services. Frequently Asked Questions What is Tall Poppy Syndrome in business? Tall Poppy Syndrome is the social instinct to resent or pull back from someone who visibly outgrows their peer group. In business, it often shows up as friends and early acquaintances becoming quieter supporters, not louder ones, once a founder's business starts to succeed. Why do friends struggle to support a growing business? Friendship is usually built on relative equality. When one person visibly grows through a business, a promotion, or new opportunities, that balance shifts. It is rarely malice. More often it is discomfort with a relationship that no longer feels level, and that discomfort quietly shows up as friends going elsewhere for what you sell. Should a founder stop growing to avoid Tall Poppy Syndrome? No. The answer is not to shrink to keep people comfortable. It is to understand where your early customers will realistically come from, usually people who meet you as a business owner first, and to build the structure that lets strangers trust you quickly since your oldest friends may take longer.

title: Why Nigerian Startups Fail Within Their First Five Years
excerpt: More than nine in ten Nigerian SMEs fail within five years. A structural diagnosis of why, and what separates the ones that survive.
body: Startup Structuring · Nigerian Business Why Nigerian Startups Fail Within Their First Five Years: A Structural Diagnosis Traction Outsourcing Limited July 14, 2026 5 min read Startup Structuring · Nigerian Business Every Nigerian founder has sat across from a business that was, on paper, supposed to work. A good product. A real market. A founder willing to work harder than almost anyone around them. And still, within a few years, the business quietly stopped opening its doors. Nobody wrote a press release. There was no dramatic collapse, just a slow decline in orders, a landlord who stopped getting paid on time, and eventually, silence. This is not a story about a lack of ambition. Nigeria has no shortage of ambition. It is a story about structure, and the absence of it. The Scale of the Problem The numbers here are difficult to look away from. Data from the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria and the National Bureau of Statistics shows that more than nine in ten Nigerian SMEs fail within their first five years of operation. A separate analysis tracking Nigerian startups between 2010 and 2018 put the failure rate at just over sixty percent, the highest among Africa's major business ecosystems during that period. 9 in 10 Nigerian SMEs fail within their first five years (SMEDAN/NBS) 60% Nigerian startup failure rate 2010-2018, highest in Africa's major ecosystems 4 in 10 Startup failures globally caused by building something nobody needed (CB Insights) These are not businesses that failed because Nigeria lacks customers, capital, or talent. Nigeria has all three, unevenly distributed, but present. What consistently emerges from research into these failures is a narrower, more specific set of causes: poor marketing strategy, an inability to correctly identify the paying customer, the absence of a real business plan, wrong location decisions, and what researchers plainly call managerial deficiency. None of these are about the product. All of them are about structure. The Global Pattern, Localised This is not uniquely a Nigerian problem, but Nigeria's version of it is sharper. Global research from CB Insights found that the single largest cause of startup failure worldwide is building something the market never actually needed, a pattern responsible for roughly four in ten failures. In Nigeria, that same failure mode is amplified by higher logistics costs, currency volatility, and thinner margins for error. A business in a more forgiving market can survive a few months of miscalculated demand. A Nigerian business operating on tight margins, with naira-denominated revenue and often dollar-denominated costs, frequently cannot. Several well-funded Nigerian startups have shut down or significantly scaled back in recent years after discovering, sometimes tens of millions of dollars into operation, that their cost per transaction exceeded what customers were willing to pay. The lesson from these cases is rarely about the idea. It is almost always about the absence of a structure rigorous enough to catch the problem before the money ran out. A good idea is never the scarce resource in Nigeria. The scarce resource is the structure that lets a good idea become a sustainable business. Structure Is Not Bureaucracy There is a persistent myth among early-stage Nigerian founders that structure is something you add once you have made it, a layer of formality reserved for companies large enough to need policies and processes. This gets the sequence backwards. The businesses that survive long enough to need that formality are, almost without exception, the ones that built basic structural discipline in from the beginning. Structure, at the early stage, is not an organogram or a thick policy manual. It is a small number of unglamorous decisions made deliberately instead of by accident: A real understanding of who the paying customer is and what they can actually afford A cost structure that has been tested against realistic sales volumes rather than optimistic ones Clear ownership of who is responsible for which decisions A cash flow discipline that separates what the business owns from what the founder is personally funding Employment and governance documentation — including a proper employee handbook and role definitions — that means the business can function if a key person leaves Businesses that skip this stage tend to discover their structural gaps at the worst possible moment, usually when a cash shortfall, a key staff departure, or a sudden spike in demand exposes exactly how much of the operation was being held together informally. This is also where Corporate Restructuring becomes relevant for businesses that have already been operating for years but have never addressed the structural gaps that have been quietly accumulating. What Separates the Businesses That Survive The Nigerian businesses that make it past the five-year mark share a pattern that has little to do with luck. They price based on what their actual customer can pay, not what a customer in a more affluent market might pay. They build governance and financial discipline while still small, when the cost of fixing a mistake is a difficult conversation rather than a bankruptcy filing. They separate personal and business finances early, so a bad month does not become an existential threat. And critically, they bring in outside advisory perspective before problems become visible, not after. That last point is the one founders resist most, often for understandable reasons. Asking for structured guidance can feel like admitting the plan was incomplete. title: How to Create an Organogram for Your Nigerian Business
excerpt: A step-by-step guide to mapping reporting lines and structure, with a worked example for a real estate company.
body: Business Structure How to Create an Organogram for Your Nigerian Business Traction Outsourcing Limited July 14, 2026 4 min read Business Structure · Startup Structuring Designing a corporate organogram is not just about drawing lines on a piece of paper. It is about mapping the nervous system of your business. In our work at Traction Outsourcing Limited, we often see businesses that function like a series of busy hallways where everyone runs into everyone else, but nobody knows who owns the final outcome. A clear organogram solves this by turning chaos into intentional order. When your team members know exactly where they fit and who they answer to, you stop paying for overlapping roles and start paying for clear results. Step 1: Audit Your Operational Reality Do not start by drawing a dream team that you hope to hire next year. Start by writing down every task your business completes today. Who manages the daily finances? Who handles client communication? Who makes the final decision when a project stalls? Map the functions that currently exist. If you find that one person is doing the work of three departments, that is your first insight. An organogram must reflect the actual flow of work, not just the desired aesthetic. Step 2: Group Functions by Impact Once you have your list of tasks, group them into core departments. Most growing businesses in Nigeria thrive when they separate these four pillars: Operations: The people who build, maintain, or deliver the core product or service. Finance & Administration: The gatekeepers of the budget, legal compliance, and internal office stability. Growth & Sales: The engine responsible for new revenue and client relationships. Talent & Culture: The team that ensures the right people are in the right seats and that the workplace remains a place where people want to stay. Step 3: Define Reporting Lines and Authority This is where most structures fail. You must decide if your culture is top-down or collaborative. For a small business, a flat structure might work. As you scale, you need vertical accountability. Every person must have one clear supervisor. If an employee reports to two managers, you have created a bottleneck where decisions go to die. Step 4: Keep It Scalable Build your organogram to be modular. If you are a startup, you might have one person acting as both the Sales Lead and the Customer Support Manager. That is fine. Just ensure the organogram shows these as two distinct functional boxes even if one person occupies both. This way, when the time comes to hire, you simply slice the role in half and bring on a new person to take over the support function. Consider This Example: A Real Estate Company Imagine you work with a young real estate management firm. You might organize it this way: the Director sits at the top, and underneath, three primary leads carry the business. Sample Organogram for a Real Estate Management Firm Director Operations Lead Property maintenance, listings, site inspections, vendor negotiations, contractor relations Sales & Brokerage Lead Property listings, client tours, partnerships & communication, contract agreements Finance & Admin Lead Rent collection, disbursement protocols, cost & expenditure management, legal paperwork If you are just starting, you might be all three leads. You draw the boxes for all three, but you write your own name in each. As the business grows, you hire a person for each box. The structure stays the same, but the burden on your personal capacity decreases. Your organogram is a living document. If your business is failing to hit its targets, the answer is often found in the lines you drew between the boxes. Review It Like You Mean It Review your organogram from time to time, usually every six months or annually. Remove the friction, clarify the reporting, and give your people the space to execute their roles and achieve their targets with brutal execution. This Is a Functional Organogram What has been described above is known as a functional organogram . There are three other types, hierarchical, flat, and matrix, however every business between zero and three years old should focus on the functional organogram. During this stage of your company's growth, you want to improve employee effectiveness at work, efficiency at handling tasks, and job satisfaction. You want to lay less emphasis on who wields what authority and more on who gets what done. If you have not yet registered the business itself, start there first. title: How to Write an Employee Handbook for a Nigerian SME
excerpt: Most Nigerian SMEs run on memory instead of policy. Here is why a handbook is one of the highest-leverage documents a growing business can build.
body: ← Back to Articles HR Advisory How to Write an Employee Handbook for a Nigerian SME Traction Outsourcing Limited July 14, 2026 4 min read HR Compliance · Nigerian Business A client once called us in the middle of a crisis that had nothing to do with sales, cash flow, or competition. Two staff members had gotten into a dispute in front of customers. One had missed work repeatedly without explanation. The business owner wanted to know what she could do about it. When we asked what her disciplinary policy said about repeated absenteeism, there was a long pause. There was no policy. There had never been one. Every decision about conduct, leave, and discipline had been made in the moment, based on mood, memory, and whichever version of fairness felt right that day. This is not a rare situation. It is the default condition of most growing Nigerian businesses. Why This Keeps Happening Academic research into HR practices among Nigerian SMEs consistently points to the same pattern: human resource decisions are rarely handled by a dedicated function. In the large majority of small and medium businesses, HR decisions rest entirely with the owner or managing director, made informally and reactively rather than through any documented framework. There is nothing unusual about this. Most businesses start as one person doing everything, and structure tends to arrive only after growth has already made the absence of structure painful. The cost of that delay shows up in ways owners do not always connect back to the missing policy. Recent workforce data shows that a majority of Nigerian employers report real difficulty finding candidates whose expectations, skills, and conduct match what the business actually needs. Some of that mismatch is about skill. A significant part of it is about expectations that were never written down in the first place, so no one, including the employer, was ever entirely sure what "meeting expectations" meant. What a Handbook Actually Does An employee handbook is not a formality for businesses that have "made it." It is a governance tool, and it does three specific jobs that nothing else in a small business does as efficiently. It removes ambiguity before conflict arrives. Disputes over lateness, leave, dress code, or termination almost always escalate faster when there is no written standard to point to. A handbook converts what would otherwise be a personal disagreement between an owner and a staff member into a question of whether documented policy was followed. That shift alone defuses a large share of workplace conflict before it starts. It protects the business legally. Nigerian labour law gives employers real obligations around termination notice, working hours, and conditions of service. A business without a handbook is not exempt from those obligations; it is simply operating without evidence that it has communicated them. When a dispute reaches a labour office or a court, the absence of a documented policy tends to be read against the employer, regardless of how reasonable the underlying decision actually was. It sets the culture before the culture sets itself. Every business has a culture, whether or not anyone designed it. Left undocumented, culture tends to be shaped by whoever is loudest, whoever has been there longest, or whoever the owner likes best. A handbook lets you decide, in advance and in writing, what kind of workplace you are actually building. What Belongs in a Nigerian SME Handbook A functional handbook for a growing Nigerian business does not need to be a two-hundred-page corporate manual. It needs to be complete enough to answer the questions that come up most often, and specific enough that no one has to guess. At minimum, it should cover: working hours and attendance expectations, leave entitlements including annual, sick, and maternity or paternity leave, a clear code of conduct, a disciplinary procedure with defined steps rather than vague language, grounds and process for termination, confidentiality obligations, and a grievance channel that lets staff raise concerns without fear of retaliation. Each of these should be written in plain language that a new hire can read once and actually understand, not legal phrasing borrowed from a template with no relevance to how the business actually runs. The Real Cost of Skipping This Step Business owners often delay writing a handbook because it feels like a task for later, once the company is "big enough" to need one. In practice, the businesses that suffer most from the absence of a handbook are the ones still small enough that one bad hire, one mishandled dispute, or one inconsistent decision can meaningfully damage morale across the entire team. A ten-person company has far less room to absorb the fallout of an unclear termination than a two-hundred-person one does. The smaller the business, the higher the relative cost of getting people decisions wrong, and the more a handbook actually matters. Building It Properly A handbook that is copied from the internet and never adapted to your actual business is close to useless. It needs to reflect your real working hours, your real leave structure, your real disciplinary process, and Nigerian labour law as it applies to your specific sector and state. Getting this right the first time saves you from having to rebuild it later, usually in the middle of a dispute, which is the worst possible time to be writing policy. Traction Outsourcing has built handbooks, codes of conduct, and full HR policy frameworks for businesses across manufacturing, hospitality, real estate, and professional services in Nigeria. We know what belongs in yours, and what does not. Do not wait for a crisis to discover you have no policy to point to. Let us build an employee handbook that actually reflects how your business runs. Get Your Handbook Built Common Questions Why does a Nigerian SME need an employee handbook? Without a written handbook, policy exists only in the founder's memory, applied inconsistently and impossible to enforce fairly. A handbook turns informal understanding into a document every employee can be held to equally. What should be included in a Nigerian employee handbook? A working handbook covers company policy, conduct expectations, leave and attendance rules, disciplinary procedure, and the practical day-to-day questions new employees actually ask, not just a legal boilerplate. What happens if a business skips having an employee handbook? Disputes get settled inconsistently, expectations vary by manager, and the business has no documented standard to point to when a disagreement over conduct or policy ends up in front of a court or tribunal. title: The Dangers of Proximity to Success
excerpt: Access without preparation is a trap dressed up as opportunity. A true story about what happens when proximity replaces a real financial foundation.
body: ← Back to Articles Business Advisory The Dangers of Proximity to Success Traction Outsourcing Limited July 14, 2026 4 min read Workplace Psychology · Leadership A couple of years ago, one hot afternoon, I met Rita in Abuja. She ran a small restaurant in a village in Kurudu. At that time, I was working on a project on one of our sites and I had not had breakfast. When I ordered, I was not expecting much from the makeshift restaurant shed that could barely fit seven people. As a result, I was surprised that her food was great, the surroundings were clean, and notably, her English was superb. I struck up a conversation with her about how good her food was, and she went on to tell me about how she was a chef. One thing led to another, and we found ourselves talking about the restaurants she visited in Germany, Australia, the UK, and so many other countries. I was curious, of course, how you could visit all the dream countries of an average Nigerian and still be selling tantalizing Jollof rice in a makeshift shed in a village. Rita explained that she worked with a boss who gave her access. Within three months of working with him, she got her passport and could travel with him locally on private jets and internationally on commercial airlines. Within a year, she found herself spending all her salary and allowances trying to meet up with the image and standard of those she found around her. When he finally had to leave Nigeria, she struggled to maintain the lifestyle. She struggled to fit in with her own people, the same people she had before she got the job. When she started a restaurant immediately after, she targeted the same people in her boss's financial and social class. They never came. She burned through her savings and had to face reality. That reality is her current restaurant in Kurudu village. Her story helped me understand a vital truth about unmetered proximity to success: access, without preparation, is a trap dressed up as an opportunity. When Proximity Becomes a Distortion If you look closely around our professional circles, you will realize Rita is not an isolated case. Her story is a quiet pattern playing out all the time. There is a well-documented psychological principle behind what happened to her. Social Comparison Theory, which dates back to the 1950s, argues that when we do not have a clear baseline for who we are, we simply borrow the identity of whoever is closest to us. Upward social comparison, measuring yourself against someone doing better, can either inspire or damage you, depending on whether you genuinely believe their level of success is within your reach. For Rita, the comparison was not gradual. It was total immersion. She was not just observing success from a distance; she was sitting inside it, traveling inside it, and eating inside it every single day. Without a baseline framework for how that world actually operated, her mind did the only thing it could do: it started treating that borrowed world as her own. This is where the danger begins. Proximity without context does not teach you how successful people think. It teaches you how they spend. We see it all the time with lifestyle inflation. It is that subtle shift where luxuries slowly start feeling like basic necessities. For Rita, the process was even more insidious because the income was not even hers. She was consuming a lifestyle funded by someone else's wealth, in someone else's name, on someone else's timeline. And when that person left, the lifestyle did not leave quietly. It left a void she felt compelled to fill. Lifestyle creep is incredibly common among young adults who experience a sudden jump in access or income. What makes it dangerous for many Nigerians who find themselves in similar positions is that the spending is not driven by an actual increase in earnings. It is driven purely by an increase in exposure. There is a massive gulf between the two. The Numbers Behind the Pattern Rita's story might feel deeply personal, but the data confirms it is structural. Data on Nigerian SMEs shows an overwhelming majority fold within the first five years, mirroring global trends where nearly half of business failures happen simply because there is no real market demand for what they are selling. This is rarely a story about bad products. It is a story about targeting the wrong people. When Rita opened her restaurant, she knew how to cook. Her food was genuinely good. What she did not know was her customer. She had spent so much time in the orbit of wealth that she had lost the ability to accurately see the market she actually belonged to. She aimed her pricing, her aesthetic, and her expectations at a clientele that had no particular reason to drive to Kurudu for a meal. Many Nigerian businesses collapse not because of a lack of skill or effort, but because of miscalibrated expectations and a fundamental misunderstanding of who their customers are and how much those customers are actually willing to spend. This is the second danger of unmetered proximity to success. It does not just distort your personal spending; it distorts your professional judgment. It recalibrates your entire sense of what is normal, what is achievable, and who you are building for. What Rita's Story Tells Us About Our Careers These lessons apply whether you are a student, a climbing professional, or an entrepreneur trying to scale. Access is not the same as preparation. Being close to success is not the same as being ready for it. Rita had access to business-class travel, fine dining, and high-level conversations, but none of that translated into capital, systems, or business knowledge when she needed it. Proximity gave her exposure, not a foundation. Your environment shapes your baseline without your permission. When the people around you set a lavish standard, your brain quietly adopts that standard as the bare minimum. You stop seeing it as exceptional and start seeing it as normal. This happens gradually to everyone. The only question is whether you are self-aware enough to notice it happening before making irreversible financial decisions. Knowing your actual market is a strategy, not a compromise. Rita's restaurant in Kurudu is not a failure of ambition; it is a failure of targeting. There is a thriving market in Kurudu, and she is successfully serving it today. The tragedy is not where she ended up. The tragedy is that she spent her life savings chasing a customer who was never coming, when the customers who would genuinely value her work were right in front of her. Knowing your market is the single most important strategic decision you can make. The Advisory Gap Nobody Talks About What Rita needed, and what many people in her situation need, was not more access. It was structured guidance. She needed someone to sit with her before she opened that restaurant and ask the uncomfortable questions: Who is your customer? What can they afford? What are you building toward, and what do you actually have right now to build with? That kind of raw, grounded conversation is rare. Most people navigate their careers and businesses based entirely on what they see around them, what their oga is doing, what their colleagues are spending, and what their peers seem to have. Very few people have access to honest, structured advisory support that helps them separate where they are from where they are going, and build a realistic bridge between the two. This is exactly the work we do at Traction Outsourcing. Alongside a team of experienced professionals, we offer career and business advisory services designed to help individuals and organizations build from a place of clarity rather than comparison. Whether you are a young professional trying to figure out your next move, an entrepreneur preparing to launch, or someone who has found themselves caught in a reality shift and needs a hard reset, the conversation starts by understanding your actual reality, not the one you have been borrowing. Rita's food is still good. It was always good. What changed the outcome of her story was not her skill; it was the absence of a plan rooted in truth. You do not have to make that same mistake. Ready for an honest conversation about where you are and where you are genuinely headed? An advisory session might be the most grounding investment you make this year. Being close to successful people or opportunities can create the illusion of readiness without the substance behind it, access is mistaken for preparation, and the gap only becomes visible once real pressure tests it. Why does access without preparation often fail? Opportunity without a real financial or business foundation underneath it tends to collapse under its own weight, since proximity can open a door but cannot substitute for the capability needed to walk through it. title: The Real Cost of a Bad Hire in Nigeria (And How to Avoid It)
excerpt: A bad hire costs far more than a salary. What the data says about the true cost of hiring wrong, and how structured recruitment prevents it.
body: Recruitment · Talent Management The Real Cost of a Bad Hire in Nigeria (And How to Avoid It) Traction Outsourcing Limited July 14, 2026 4 min read Recruitment · Nigerian Business A growing Abuja business needs an operations manager urgently. The founder is stretched thin, interviews are rushed, and a confident candidate with an impressive CV gets the offer within a week. Four months later, projects are behind schedule, two junior staff have quietly resigned, and the founder is back where they started, except now with a severance package to pay, a damaged team, and the same vacant role still open. This pattern repeats across Nigerian businesses more often than most owners admit. The cost of a bad hire rarely announces itself. It shows up slowly, in missed deadlines and quiet resignations, long after the decision that caused it. What the Data Actually Says The most widely cited benchmark comes from the United States Department of Labor, which estimates that a bad hire costs a business a minimum of thirty percent of that employee's first-year salary, purely in direct replacement costs. That figure is described as conservative for a reason. The Society for Human Resource Management puts the fuller cost, once lost productivity and management time are included, between fifty and two hundred percent of annual salary depending on seniority, with executive-level bad hires sitting at the top of that range. 30% Minimum direct replacement cost as a share of the employee's first-year salary (US DoL) 200% Upper end of total cost including lost productivity and management time for senior roles (SHRM) 3 in 4 Employers who admit to having hired the wrong person for a role at some point (CareerBuilder) These figures were built around Western labour markets, but the underlying mechanics translate directly to Nigeria, often with the damage compounding faster. A Nigerian business rehiring for the same role a second time within a year is not just repeating a recruitment fee. It is absorbing the cost of statutory notice or severance, the delay in productivity while the seat sits empty again, and the reputational cost among remaining staff who watched the first hire fail. There is a local dimension that pure salary multipliers do not capture. Recent workforce research shows that a majority of Nigerian employers report genuine difficulty finding candidates who match what the role actually requires. That skills mismatch pushes businesses toward rushed hiring simply to fill a seat. And rushed hiring is precisely the condition under which bad hires happen. The salary paid to a bad hire is the smallest part of the loss. The larger damage comes from three places that rarely appear on a balance sheet. Where the Damage Actually Comes From Management time. A manager or founder dealing with an underperforming hire spends a disproportionate share of their week correcting mistakes, having difficult conversations, and redoing work that should not need redoing. That is time not spent on growth, on clients, or on the parts of the business that actually generate revenue. Team morale. A bad hire who is allowed to stay too long sends a quiet signal to the rest of the team about what the business is willing to tolerate. Strong performers notice when weak performance goes unaddressed, and some of them start looking elsewhere. This connects directly to the accountability culture the business has built, or failed to build. The second hiring cycle. Every bad hire that fails means the business is effectively paying for the same vacancy twice: once for the person who did not work out, and again for the replacement search. If the replacement search is conducted the same way as the first, the outcome is likely to be the same. Why Structured Recruitment Prevents This Most bad hires are not the result of bad luck. They are the result of a hiring process that relied too heavily on a strong interview performance and too little on structured evaluation. Research on hiring methodology consistently shows that structured interviews, where every candidate is assessed against the same defined criteria, predict job performance far more reliably than open-ended conversation. The businesses that avoid repeat bad hires tend to share the same discipline: They define the role and its success metrics in detail before the search begins, not during it They run every candidate through the same structured process instead of relying on gut feeling They verify claims through reference and background checks rather than taking a CV at face value Where the role is critical, they use an experienced recruitment partner who has the vetting infrastructure and the distance to evaluate objectively This is exactly what ATH Recruiters , a brand of Traction Outsourcing Limited, is built to do. A bad hire costs significantly more than the salary paid. In Nigeria, the damage often compounds faster because of re-advertising costs, re-onboarding time, and the morale impact on the team that watched the first hire fail. What causes a bad hire in Nigeria? Bad hires most often come from rushed, informal recruitment: vague job descriptions, no structured interview process, and no clear definition of what success in the role looks like before the search begins.
